Thither
THITH-er
adverb
From the Old English thider, “to that place,” formed on the same demonstrative stem as that and there; hence motion toward a place away from the speaker — the answer to whither, as there answers where.

Biblical Definition

Thither is the old adverb of motion toward — not there, which marks rest in a place, but thither, which marks the going to it. The KJV keeps the distinction our speech has lost, and the loss is not small, for Scripture is full of men on the way to somewhere. The manslayer has a thither: the LORD appointed cities of refuge “that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares” (Num 35:11) — a place named beforehand, a road prepared, a gate that stands open to the pursued. So Christ is the refuge to which the guilty run. Moses had a thither he was not given: the LORD showed him the land from Nebo and said, “thou shalt not go over thither” (Deu 34:4) — the servant sees the promise and the greater Joshua brings the people in. The word governs the doctrine of the effectual Word: as the rain “returneth not thither, but watereth the earth” (Isa 55:10), so God’s word does not go out and come back empty but accomplishes that which He pleases. And it falls with terrible weight from the lips of Christ upon the unbelieving: “where I am, thither ye cannot come” (Joh 7:34). There is a place whither the Lord is gone and a road thither, and the man who will not come by Him shall seek and not find. Every soul is travelling somewhere. The only question the word asks is whether the thither is the refuge or the dark.

Webster 1828 Definition

To that place; toward that place — the adverb of motion toward, answering to whither.

expand to see more

THITHER, to that place; used of motion toward, not of rest in.

From the Saxon thider, of the same stem as that and there.

It answers to whither, as there answers to where.

The slayer fled thither, to the appointed city of refuge (Num 35:11).

Christ says of Himself, “where I am, thither ye cannot come” (Joh 7:34).

Key Scripture

Num 35:11 — "Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares."

Deu 34:4 — "And the LORD said unto him, This is the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying, I will give it unto thy seed: I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither."

Isa 55:10 — "For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater:"

Joh 7:34 — "Ye shall seek me, and shall not find me: and where I am, thither ye cannot come."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but a plain word of motion toward; it recovers that every soul is travelling somewhere, and that the refuge has a road to it.

expand to see more

The word rebukes an age with no thither. Modern speech has collapsed whither and thither into a flat where, and the flattening of the grammar has followed the flattening of the life: men move endlessly and arrive nowhere, calling the motion itself the meaning. Scripture will not have it. The manslayer ran to a named city on a cleared road; Israel marched toward a sworn land; the rain falls and does not return thither empty. Motion in the Bible has a terminus, appointed by God before the runner ever set out.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that there are only two destinations, and Christ is the road to the one worth reaching. The LORD appointed cities of refuge that the slayer might flee thither and live — and the gospel appoints a refuge for men who have shed blood far worse, with the gate standing open and the avenger behind. But there is also the word of Joh 7:34: “where I am, thither ye cannot come.” The Lord has gone to the Father, and the man who refuses the only way shall seek Him and not find Him. Let a man ask not whether he is moving but whither, and by what road.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means “to that place” — motion toward, as distinct from rest in a place.

expand to see more

Thither — Old English thider, “to that place.”

Built on the demonstrative stem of that and there.

It marks motion toward; there marks rest in the place.

It is the answer to the question whither, “to what place?”

The slayer fled thither to the city of refuge and lived (Num 35:11).

Usage

"The slayer fled thither: God named the refuge and cleared the road before ever the blood was shed."

"Moses saw the land but might not go over thither — the servant sees; the greater Joshua brings in."

"The rain returneth not thither empty, and neither does the word that goeth out of God’s mouth."
